title: LLM codegen fails and how to stop 'em — Danilo Campos, PostHog

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk centers on the PostHog Wizard, an autonomous codegen agent that writes software integrations for 15,000 monthly users, with failure modes and mitigations specific to code generation. The wizard is a coding assistant for developers integrating PostHog, built atop developer-platform infrastructure including the Claude agent SDK and PostHog's LLM gateway. The wizard is a production system with active users, and the talk covers post-deployment maintenance practices like post-run interrogation and tool permission lockdowns. The talk assumes working knowledge of LLMs, agents, and software integration but remains accessible to practicing engineers. This is a conference presentation delivered on the AI Engineer channel. summary: Danilo Campos of PostHog shares lessons from building the PostHog Wizard, an autonomous codegen tool that 15,000 people per month use to integrate PostHog, saving users approximately 2 hours each. He identifies several major failure modes and corresponding mitigations. First, model rot: models are snapshots of the world months ago and don't track fast-moving software. The solution is loading fresh markdown documentation into context, letting the agent select relevant docs from posthog.com. Second, weird architecture: models trained on poorly structured projects produce odd integration patterns. PostHog maintains 'model airplanes'—thin, token-efficient reference projects across frameworks that have the correct shape of an integration, guiding the agent consistently. These are flattened into a single markdown file and included as supplemental content in skill files generated by a context service. Third, excessive improvisation: 15,000 monthly integrations could yield 15,000 unique approaches. The solution is breadcrumbing—staged discovery of business-value files, then events, then implementation. Fourth, human error: contradictory or incorrect tool instructions cause silent failures, including hundreds of runs with a missing tool and JavaScript instructions sent for Python projects. The mitigation is post-run inference-time interrogation. Fifth, security: early versions read .env files and sent contents to the cloud. The fix is fine-grained tool control with purpose-built tools that never expose secrets. Campos argues that value has shifted from code to prose: the wizard is 90% markdown files, 8% tools for markdown processing, and the rest agent harness. Code is a depreciating asset that loses value when new models drop, while great prose appreciates—better models extract more from existing prose. He likens agents to octopuses that can wiggle through problems, advising against over-constraining them; instead, provide sufficient information and sequence it properly. Infrastructure details include the Claude agent SDK wrapped in a CLI, free inference via PostHog's LLM gateway, and skill files from a context service. Campos notes this is early days for agent-as-a-service, with challenges like Claude code storing information in unexpected places. He emphasizes human maintainers are the biggest threat to agent success due to limited, fragmentary context.

sections.title: Opening & PostHog Wizard Introduction
sections.summary: Campos introduces himself and the PostHog Wizard, which 15,000 people per month use to get a working PostHog integration, saving 2 hours of manual work. He notes recent unprompted positive social media posts as evidence it works.

sections.title: Model Rot & Fresh Documentation
sections.summary: Models are snapshots months out of date. PostHog addresses model rot by letting the agent use tools to select fresh markdown documentation from posthog.com and load it into context, compensating for stale training data that previously caused invented APIs and keys.

sections.title: Model Airplanes for Correct Architecture
sections.summary: Agents can make strange architectural decisions from poor training examples. PostHog maintains 'model airplanes'—thin, token-efficient reference projects across frameworks with correct integration shapes (e.g., non-functional but properly shaped auth), ensuring agents consistently apply correct patterns.

sections.title: Breadcrumbing to Limit Improvisation
sections.summary: To prevent 15,000 different integration approaches, PostHog breadcrumbs the agent through staged discovery: first finding business-value files, then identifying interesting events without writing code, then implementing with loaded documentation. Business code 'casts a huge shadow' and is reliably detectable.

sections.title: Human Error & Agent Interrogation
sections.summary: Human maintainers are the biggest threat to agent outcomes due to limited, fragmentary context. Examples include contradictory MCP tool instructions, a missing tool referenced across hundreds of runs, and JavaScript instructions sent for Python projects. The solution is post-run inference-time interrogation asking the agent what could have been done better.

sections.title: Security & Tool Permission Lockdown
sections.summary: Running agents on others' machines demands trust. Early wizard versions read .env files and sent contents to the cloud. PostHog locked down tool permissions and built a purpose-built ENV tool that only checks key presence and writes values without exposing secrets to inference.

sections.title: From Code to Prose: Where Value Lives Now
sections.summary: Campos argues the era of coding your way out of problems is over. Code is a depreciating asset—when a new model drops, existing code holds the same or declining value. The wizard is 90% markdown files, 8% tools for markdown processing, and the rest agent harness. Plain text prose is where value now lives: great prose written today appreciates when better models arrive, as they can do more with it.

sections.title: Agent as Octopus: Don't Over-Constrain
sections.summary: Campos likens agents to octopuses that can wiggle and squeeze into tight corners. Rather than heavily scaffolding agent behavior, the approach is to step back, provide sufficient information, and sequence it so the agent does the right thing and makes people happy—aside from security guardrails.

sections.title: Q&A: Skill Files, Infrastructure & Closing
sections.summary: Campos explains that model airplanes are flattened into a single markdown file by a context service and included as supplemental reference in skill files, alongside documentation prose. The wizard uses the Claude agent SDK wrapped in a CLI, with free inference via PostHog's LLM gateway. He notes it's early days for agent-as-a-service, citing challenges where Claude code stored information in unexpected places and broke for users.
